hints: Focus on what a Bronsted-Lowry base actually does, it must accept a proton ($\text{H}^+$) from another species.
Look at reaction B and track water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ gains one $\text{H}^+$ to become $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$.
Check the other equations for who gains the proton, in one of them ammonia does it instead of water.
walkthrough:
**Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definition**

A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. An acid is a proton donor.

So look for: $$\text{base} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{conjugate acid}$$

**Test reaction B**

Water gains a proton from phosphoric acid to form hydroxonium.

$$\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$
Here $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ accepts $\text{H}^+$, so it is the base. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ donates $\text{H}^+$, so it is the acid.

**Confirm the others do not fit**

In A there is no proton transfer, it is redox to make $\text{H}_2$. In C there is no proton transfer, it is oxide plus water. In D it is $\text{NH}_3$ that accepts the proton to make $\text{NH}_4^+$, so ammonia is the base, not water.

options.A: This is a redox reaction, not a Bronsted-Lowry acid-base reaction. Sodium is oxidised and water is reduced to $\text{H}_2$. Water does not accept a proton to form a conjugate acid here.
options.B: Water accepts a proton ($\text{H}^+$) from $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ to form $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. Accepting a proton is exactly the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base.
options.C: This is an acid-base oxide reaction forming $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$. There is no proton donor and no $\text{H}^+$ transfer from an acid to water, so water is not acting as a proton acceptor.
options.D: Here $\text{NH}_3$ accepts a proton to form $\text{NH}_4^+$, so ammonia is the Bronsted-Lowry base. The aqua complex donates a proton, meaning a coordinated water molecule is actually acting as the Bronsted-Lowry acid.
